title: Holiness and failure together
hookLine: the middle ages had both inquisitions and hospitals, crusades and Francis

cards: A farmer's servants come to him with bad news. An enemy has sown weeds in the wheat field while everyone slept, and now the two are coming up together. Shall we go and pull them out?
No, says the farmer. You'll tear up the wheat with them. Let both grow until the harvest.
Jesus tells that story in Matthew's Gospel, and near the end of this long walk through the middle ages, it's a useful way of looking back.

teach.b: First, the failure, said plainly. These centuries had crusades, with massacres along the way. They had inquisitions, courts that questioned and punished people for their beliefs.
They had Jews blamed and killed in times of plague, popes who schemed for money and power, and a king who emptied the monasteries. None of that needs softening.

teach.h: THE HOLINESS, IN THE SAME YEARS.
teach.b: Second, the holiness, in the same years. The Rule of Saint Benedict tells monks that care for the sick comes before everything, and that the sick are to be served as Christ himself.
Elizabeth of Hungary founded a hospital and nursed the sick in it. Francis walked unarmed into a sultan's camp in the middle of a crusade. Julian of Norwich heard that all shall be well.
Third, the temptation: keeping only one list. Some tell these centuries as nothing but darkness, others as a golden age. Both are easier to carry than the truth.
Fourth, how the Church describes itself.

You heard it with the Renaissance popes: the Second Vatican Council calls the Church at once holy and always in need of being purified. Set that beside the parable, and it looks a lot like the farmer's field.
The Douay-Rheims calls the weeds cockle. The servants want a clean field now.
The farmer says: "Suffer both to grow until the harvest." It isn't permission to excuse the weeds. In the story, the harvest still comes, and the weeds are still weeds.
It's a warning against pretending that only one of them ever grew.

how: Catholics confess sins personally in the sacrament of reconciliation, and the Church has also made public acts of repentance for wrongs done by its members in the past, while continuing to honor the saints of the same centuries.

games.q: you're the farmer. your servants find weeds coming up in the wheat and want to pull them out tonight. what do you say?
o: let both grow until the harvest.
burn the whole field and start again.
games.why: he tells them to wait, or they'll tear up the wheat with the weeds. the harvest still comes, and the weeds are still weeds.

practice: Bring to mind something you belong to: a family, a church, a country, a team.
Name one real failure in it, without excuses; then, without letting go of the first, name one real goodness, and keep both in view the way the farmer kept the whole field.
If you pray, offer both to God together; if you don't, simply hold them side by side.

wordCard.voice: Cockle. The Douay-Rheims word for the weeds in Jesus's parable, left to grow beside the wheat until harvest, the way holiness and failure grew together in the medieval Church. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the weeds in the parable, a weed that grows up among the wheat; the Douay-Rheims calls it cockle.

carryVoice: Your line: both are true. The whole field, wheat and cockle together. Day eight hundred forty-five.
